The console’s latest upgrade finally activates its dormant Wi-Fi hardware enabling a handful of new features.﻿.

Sources indicate that analogue has long been good at expanding the features and functionality of its consoles through regular firmware updates, but installing those updates has always required moving files around with a memory card. That’s no longer the case with the Analogue 3D, the company’s modernized version of the Nintendo 64. Although the console has had Wi-Fi hardware since day one, it’s only now been finally activated through the last update you’ll need to install with a memory card.

Analogue released the version 1.6.0 firmware for the Analogue 3D yesterday which adds support for 2.4GHz, 5GHz, mixed, and hidden Wi-Fi networks. Once the upgrade is installed the Wi-Fi setup process will begin automatically when the console is booted, but there’s now an added Wi-Fi section in the Analogue 3D’s settings menu for updating passwords and other details later.

Sources indicate that the console’s new Wi-Fi capabilities add a couple of useful features at launch. In the future the Analogue 3D will be able to download and install firmware updates so it automatically keeps itself up to date. The new wireless capabilities enable automatic date and time settings based on your time zone, too, and in the privacy section of the console’s settings menu you’ll now find an option for sharing “anonymous usage and analytics data” with Analogue to help further improve its hardware.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (709 w)

Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

Nimble enters the item-tracking market with eco-friendly luggage tags and keychains

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (709 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that as Google steps up its competition with Apple in the item-tracking market, smaller brands are also looking to carve out a piece of the category.
  • Founded in 2018 by former Mophie executives, the California-based organization confirmed Thursday that it’s expanding into the category with “Trace,” a seven-product collection of item trackers designed to blend tracking technology into everyday accessories.
  • Nimble’s fresh collection arrives as competition in the Bluetooth tracking market continues to heat up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as Google steps up its competition with Apple in the item-tracking market, smaller brands are also looking to carve out a piece of the category. The latest entrant is Nimble, the sustainable accessories brand best known for its charging products.

Founded in 2018 by former Mophie executives, the California-based organization confirmed Thursday that it’s expanding into the category with “Trace,” a seven-product collection of item trackers designed to blend tracking technology into everyday accessories.

Nimble’s fresh collection arrives as competition in the Bluetooth tracking market continues to heat up. Apple’s AirTag helped popularize the category, while Google recently introduced its first-party tracker, the $29 Pixel Tag, powered by its Find Hub network. Meanwhile, established third-party players, such as Chipolo and Pebblebee, continue to expand their lineups.

Nimble is taking a slightly different approach. Rather than introducing another standalone tracker to attach to a set of keys or slip into a bag, the manufacturer has integrated tracking technology directly into practical accessories, including wallets, keychains, luggage tags, and passport covers.

Recent findings suggest that the lineup includes seven products, ranging from the $14.95 Trace Tag, which features a replaceable coin-cell battery, to the $49.95 Trace Folio, a passport cover with built-in rechargeable tracking. Other options include the Trace Keyfob ($19.95), Trace Slim Wallet Card ($29.95), Trace Keychain ($29.95), Trace Luggage Tag ($39.95), and Trace Wallet ($39.95).

The entire collection is compatible with both Apple’s Find My and Google’s Find Hub networks.

Ross Howe, co-founder and CEO of Nimble, told us that the company’s approach is designed to differentiate its products from traditional trackers.

“Most locators are built as utility gadgets, not as things you want to own. Few were asking why the locator couldn’t just be the nice object itself. So, for example, we made a wallet findable instead of making a tracker that fits a wallet. We also thought more options should be rechargeable.”.

It has been revealed that the Trace Luggage Tag and Trace Folio are arguably the most interesting products in the collection. Dedicated luggage tags and passport covers with built-in tracking remain relatively uncommon, giving Nimble an opportunity to stand out in a market. There are only a few alternatives, including Spotminder’s $59 passport cover with Apple Find My support, which is $10 more than Nimble’s option. Knog Scout offers a luggage tag, although I find its design a little too bulky.

Recent findings suggest that rechargeability is another appealing aspect of Nimble’s new collection. Several models support USB-C or wireless charging, offering an alternative to the disposable batteries found in many traditional trackers. Howe states battery life lasts for “months,” with the Trace Keyfob, for example, rated for approximately six months on a charge.

Sustainability is another major part of Nimble’s pitch. Staying true to its roots, the organization has incorporated eco-friendly materials throughout the collection, including recycled plastics and plant-based, vegan aloe leather. The products have also undergone third-party testing for chemicals of concern.

“We’ve spent the last two years going through the chemistry of our products line by line to remove or limit as many harmful ingredients as possible. Trace is the first collection designed specifically to meet these higher standards. We’re not 100% yet, but the independent labs checking our work will help us get there,” Howe said.

Sources indicate that the collection is available now through its website and Amazon. All seven products come in five color options: Black, Stone, Tangerine, Plum, and Teal.

#1333. Mouse fight club might explain why we like to watch violent things

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1004 w)
📖 Baca

Mouse fight club might explain why we like to watch violent things

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1004 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s something about watching violent events that broadly appeals to us, whether it’s the latest John Wick movie, a video game, or a live UFC bout.
  • Industry observers note that the team assigned male mice randomly to three different groups—fighters, spectators, or novices—and then subjected each group to eight days of training involving three 10-minute sessions per day.
  • It has been revealed that the ninth day was “fight night,” when all the mice had to face a daunting opponent in three 4-minute rounds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s something about watching violent events that broadly appeals to us, whether it’s the latest John Wick movie, a video game, or a live UFC bout. Scientists have debated whether watching violent things could make us more aggressive, but it could also be an adaptive survival strategy. Male mice, for instance, who watch other mice fighting learned enough about how to fight to better protect themselves (compared to mice who didn’t watch fights) when pitted against stronger, more aggressive opponents, according to a paper published in the journal Nature.

Industry observers note that the team assigned male mice randomly to three different groups—fighters, spectators, or novices—and then subjected each group to eight days of training involving three 10-minute sessions per day. The novices played with stuffed mice in isolation, while the spectators watched various pairs of fighter mice battle it out from a raised platform behind a transparent barrier—a set-up chosen to let them smell and listen to the fights as well as observe them.

It has been revealed that the ninth day was “fight night,” when all the mice had to face a daunting opponent in three 4-minute rounds. Each fight was filmed from above so that the mouse behavior could be analyzed. To monitor corresponding changes in brain activity, the team engineered the rodents’ excitatory brain cells to glow green whenever they were activated, while inhibitory brain cells glowed red. They also implanted tiny optical fibers into 12 interconnected brain regions so they could track changing activity in every brain region simultaneously.

In a recent development, how did they get the mice to fight? “Mice are naturally territorial,” co-author Jorge Iravedra-Garcia of Princeton University told Ars. “A traditional behavioral assay that experimenters use is called resident intruder. You just drop mice that are bred to be slightly weaker, and a little bit more docile, into the home cage of strains we know are more on the aggressive side. Those strains are typically very good at just naturally evoking that behavior.”.

So the fights weren’t entirely fair. “We tip the scales in favor of having a clear winner and a clear loser by having the clear winner be at home, be bigger, and be more experienced,” co-author Annegret Falkner, also of Princeton, told Ars. “We really wanted to show that these changes are adaptive in some way. Animals don’t know what the outcome of a fight is before they enter it. So we set up a situation where the outcome is a little bit more uncertain for the mouse.”.

The results: the spectator mice ended up being better prepared for fight night—despite being weaker, less aggressive strains—because they watched fighter mice during the training sessions. Specifically, both spectators and fighters spent less time with their backs turned toward opponents than novice mice, and were also quicker to attack. They also used similar moves. Granted, they weren’t quite as skilled as their fighter-mouse brethren; practical experience still mattered. But they learned enough through observation to perform better than the novices.

That behavioral change was mirrored in the neural data: the brains of the spectator mice altered to more closely resemble the brains of the fighting mice across all 12 of the interconnected regions. During training, the spectator inhibitory cells resembled a fighter’s, while the excitatory cells were closer to those of novice mice, but that changed on fight night, when both types of cells more closely resembled those of fighting mice.

“When you’re watching a fight, you’re paying attention to many things at once,” said Iravedra-Garcia. “You’re not just simulating that aggressive behavior in your head, you’re also trying to gauge who’s dangerous, who’s not, who’s actually involved in the fight versus ‘Do I know them? Are they novel to me?’ Witnessing aggression leaves a circuit trace that changes how an animal behaves in its next conflict, and that trace looks similar to the one left by fighting itself.”.

Recent findings suggest that “They can watch males walking around all they want and none of this happens,” said Falkner. “There’s something specifically salient and arousing about attack that makes them both want to attend to it and also drives this specific plasticity mechanism. That’s one of the open questions: why is attack so sticky? Probably because it creates these adaptive behavioral changes.”.

Recent findings suggest that there have been similar studies, notably with macaques. According to Falkner, this latest study adds to that body of research by pointing to a specific mechanism for the learned behavior. “There’s this broad decrease in regions that are known to provide inhibitory control for some of these aggression control networks,” she said. “This one piece of the aggression network is really just the tip of the iceberg in terms of how global networks for aggression control respond during these observed activities. I think these subcortical subnetworks are really recurrent. It’s a tiny piece of a larger network.”.

Recent findings suggest that it’s an open question whether such findings involving mice could extend to human beings. “Although it’s difficult to draw a one-to-one parallel, these circuits are extremely conserved, especially these brain regions that seem to show this robust change in inhibitory tone,” said Falkner. “We think about violence as being maladaptive in human culture, but if you are a mouse or an animal who’s around a lot of aggression, it’s actually highly adaptive for you to be ready to fight at any particular time.” The same could be true of humans.

The authors plan to extend their research to determine whether female mice watching male mice duking it out changes their mating preferences. They also want to try to artificially induce the same brain activity changes and corresponding behavior. “It doesn’t seem that farfetched to me,” said Falkner. “I think we know the state that the circuit needs to be in to execute this particular behavioral strategy. So whatever pattern of stimulation we can use to kick this plasticity mechanism into gear seems reasonable.”.

According to recent reports, DOI: Nature, 2026. 10.1038/s41586-026-11217-9  (About DOIs).

Breaking: Pebble Index 01 AI ring review: When a single feature becomes the product

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1153 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s a whimsical side project for the smartwatch firm, but a useful one.
  • In 2009, Apple CEO Steve Jobs met with the founders of Dropbox with the intention of buying the file-sharing service.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Index 01 is the first of what Migicovsky hopes will be many small, slightly whimsical side projects made by the revived Pebble.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s a whimsical side project for the smartwatch firm, but a useful one.

In 2009, Apple CEO Steve Jobs met with the founders of Dropbox with the intention of buying the file-sharing service. As part of the negotiation, Jobs reportedly said Dropbox was a "feature, not a product," and the business couldn't survive long term in its own right. That was my first thought when Pebble CEO Eric Migicovsky highlighted me the Index 01 back in January. A $75 non-smart ring that puts a tiny microphone on your finger just for speaking to your AI!? Surely, that's a (software) feature on a watch or smart ring, not a whole product you could sell in its own right. All I can say is that I'm glad I didn't say those words out loud at the time, because I'd be eating them today.

Recent findings suggest that the Index 01 is the first of what Migicovsky hopes will be many small, slightly whimsical side projects made by the revived Pebble. It's a non-smart, stainless steel ring which sits on your index finger with a single physical rubber-clad button and an RGB LED.

If you don't know your ring size and don't feel like taking a risk, you can grab a sizing kit from the company. You'll get an injection-molded set of sizers back for you to wear for a day or two to check the fit, and I'd urge you to keep a craft knife or pair of sprue cutters on hand.

As I said, the idea here is to put a physical talk-to-your device button on your index finger for the thoughts you just need to dump out of your mental cache. By default, if you hold the button and talk, your words will be sent to its homegrown AI, Index Agent, but you can also set it to be processed locally. The button has a wonderfully satisfying click, which is both great to feel and means there's so much resistance that I've only accidentally activated it once in my time wearing it. When active, you need to hold the ring less than a foot away from your mouth to concern your edict, and within about 10 seconds it'll be processed on your phone.

Industry observers note that plenty of the things that the Index 01 is doing is the sort of bread-and-butter ambient computing that's been knocking around for years. With your voice, you can leave yourself notes and reminders, add items to a shopping list or set timers, with the system working out where to place each one. There are separate panes inside the Pebble app for Notes to Self, Reminders and Shopping List, which has worked flawlessly so far, even with oblique requests.

You can, of course, also ask Index Agent to answer questions about your schedule and to pull information from the internet. I found the former to be much more reliable than the latter, and the agent managed to embarrass itself in at least one of my tests. One of my usual go-tos is to ask agents who the current manager of a soccer team is, given the volatility of such a role. During testing, Mauricio Pochettino stepped down as the manager of the US men's national team to take over a team sitting in the bottom three of the Premier League. When I asked Index who was running the US men's team, it suggested Pochettino — no great shame in not being that up to date. But, when I asked who was managing the club he was about to take over, it remarked Ruben Amorim, who was fired January 5, 2026 and has had two successors since then.

According to recent reports, now, I'm the sort of person who doesn't use ambient computing because, for me, I don't like the privacy implications of having a device which is always listening. Equally key, I know I can do whatever task I need with my fingers faster than I could render it as speech. I can set a kitchen timer on my phone in about five seconds, saying it out loud takes twice as long. But the fact Index 01 is only listening when I activate it, and that it's on my finger already, flips the script.

Inside the Pebble app, you can change the destination to whatever AI agent you use, and also change what the trigger action. So, for instance, if you'd rather trigger a web search or a webhook, you can do that, as well as hook up to an MCP server. As I said when reviewing the Pebble Time 2, the app lacks polish, as the focus is on adding functionality over gloss. And I think the target market — people who didn't just have to look up what a webhook / MCP server was — won't be deterred.

According to recent reports, pebble is an Android-first manufacturer, and the ring can do several more things when paired with that ecosystem over iOS. Double click the ring and you'll trigger music playback, a triple click advances to the next song and you can set the ring to send messages via Beeper.

As usual, Pebble has made the point that there are plenty of other devices available if you want something outside its narrow offering. In its materials, the manufacturer notes if you want a smart ring get an Oura ($399) and if you want a long-term AI recorder, get a Plaud. (The Plaud NotePin is $159, which can continuously record up to 20 hours of audio for later transcription.).

In terms of similar devices, the most obvious choice is the Wizpr Ring, which I saw at CES 2024 when it was called the Whsp Ring. The organization is at the moment fulfilling Indiegogo orders, where rings were priced at $139, but notes its retail price will be $199 when it launches. Vocci's ring will set you back $299, can record up to eight hours of conversations at a time and will let you speak to your AI agents. Just bear in mind, it comes with a monthly subscription which will only offer up unlimited transcription at the $30 a month tier. Another option is Aina's far fancier ring, which was announced at the start of November and will ship early next year for $399.

The Pebble Index 01 is nothing more than a physical manifestation of what would otherwise be a software feature. A discrete, standalone button that I'd argue nobody really needs, but it's useful enough to easily justify if you want one. I'm not going to try and dissuade you if your initial reaction was much like mine, because it's the sane and sensible thing to think. But bear in mind that, at this sort of price, it's the type of low-investment gadget that might wind up finding itself an integral part of far more people's days than anyone expects.

UnGodly is the debut game by developer Azra Games, a studio set up by former BioWare and EA executive Mark Otero. It's described as a dark fantasy action RPG, with a major story focus. It follows a mercenary called Vander, who rescues a young woman from a sinister ritual and assembles a squad of warriors called Primals to take on a sinister force that threatens the world.

Each Primal is descended from an ancient god and brings their own distinct abilities and roles to combat. There are presently more than two dozen to unlock, with more on the way, including Conan the Barbarian thanks to an official crossover collaboration.

Character progression is an important part of the game, with unique character quests and the ability to develop platonic (and even romantic) relationships with your team.

Otero says that "console games on mobile" has been an aspiration for years, and this release finally "delivers on that promise." He adds that UnGoldy offers "the same depth, fidelity, and experience you'd expect on PC or console.".

The game is at the moment available on the Google Play Store, with an enhanced experience and more precise controls for those playing on PC via Google Play Games for PC.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Samsung may be working on something more exciting than another Galaxy Z Fold or Z Flip refresh. The firm is reportedly developing a smartphone with a sliding display that can change shape depending on how you want to use it.

The latest information comes from well-known leaker Ice Universe, who shared concept renders on X that revealed the device may switch between 16:9 and 21:9 aspect ratios. The images reveal a slightly squat handset that tapers off into a more traditional smartphone shape.

As per the leak, this device could expand vertically instead of folding in half, so you get a small phone when you want it but a taller screen when you want more screen.

Samsung is developing a phone with a display that can extend from 16:9 to 21:9. Some people prefer a wider screen, while others like a taller form factor. This design could accommodate both, letting users adjust the proportions to suit what they’re doing. If Samsung can make it work, it could be a very appealing solution. Battery capacity is the big challenge, though. The sliding mechanism would take up a considerable amount of internal space, leaving less room for the battery. How much capacity could Samsung fit inside? And would it deliver enough battery life with the screen fully extended? Those are questions it needs to answer before this becomes a practical everyday device.November 11, 2026.

According to recent reports, it's not an entirely latest idea. Samsung Display has been working on rollable panels for quite some time, and Samsung even demoed a similar concept at MWC 2026. But that prototype required manual shifting and not a fully automated mechanism.

Samsung’s patent filings give us a better idea of what might be going on behind the scenes. One application consists of two sections of housing, which move relative to each other, connected by a flexible display.

Instead of consumers having to pull the screen out, it could roll around an internal mechanism and extend when needed, maybe by a motor.

Of course, fitting a motorized screen into a smartphone has some compromises. The sliding assembly occupies space inside the chassis, and this space is no longer available for the battery. A bigger screen could also mean higher power consumption when extended, making battery life a particularly notable question.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

In a recent development, samsung’s patent work reveals reinforced sliding rails and supporting slats behind the flexible panel to protect it in motion. The organization might also look at silicon-carbon battery technology to get more capacity into the tight space, just like it did to the Galaxy Z8 series. But these are still possible solutions, not confirmed specs for a finished phone.

In a recent development, samsung has not confirmed whether the device will be available in stores. Earlier reports have suggested a 2028 commercial launch could be possible, but that's a long way from being a firm commitment.

For now it suggests Samsung is looking beyond traditional foldables, exploring ways to make a phone’s screen adapt to its owner rather than the other way around.

Gemini also automatically blurs faces of bystanders in visual requests. Google says it doesn't use visuals captured for AI training or ad targeting.

Industry observers note that there’s another catch, however: it’s not universally compatible. Supported devices are newer Samsung Galaxy phones running One UI 9 based on Android 17, Google Pixel 7 and later, and iPhone 13 Pro or later.

Preorders are now available through Google, Gentle Monster, and Warby Parker ahead of its December 10 launch in the US and South Korea (Gentle Monster models only).

However, Samsung also wants to collaborate with established medical institutions in South Korea. Choi says Samsung has already started "opening up wearable sensor data to external companies with which we have signed agreements.".

Industry observers note that the goal is to standardize health data available through the Samsung Health app to deliver greater value to people. There's still a long road ahead for Samsung and its partner institutions, as the post notes the firm is working on (and providing) proofs of concept with hospitals.

According to recent reports, in the U.S., Choi notes Samsung wants to leverage its acquisition of Xealth. Xealth excels in digital health solutions for hospitals. It reduces the gap between the health data you capture on a Galaxy Watch and what your doctor sees and knows about you. Samsung says it wants to pursue deeper partnerships with U.S. hospitals through Xealth by 2030, potentially connecting users with over 100 institutions.

Samsung continues to push for better health assistance and insights, and I think this is totally worth it. If we're going to use AI to help, this is where it should be applied. It's even more worth it when you consider that your data will be shared with your hospital. This gets your doctor's eyes on your info, and they can make the judgment call that truly matters. Still a lot to be done, but this is interesting.

Samsung has more work to do on home soil to get to the same point as it is (or is going to be) in the U.S. Speaking of which, if all goes smoothly, Samsung would be able to transfer/share a user's "sleep, exercise, and blood pressure" insights from its Health app with their hospital.

According to recent reports, it's no surprise that Samsung wants to bridge a gap between owners and doctors. Last year, the company released virtual doctor visits, which you can find in the app today. Through a partnership with HealthTap, the Find Care feature helps match users with a doctor for a virtual visit. Users can also text their virtual doctor in case new symptoms appear.

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20.

Intelligent Eyewear is meant to be worn all day rather than the sunglasses-heavy approach taken by others. The frames are 40-44 grams with the weight balanced evenly.

Recent findings suggest that notably, Gemini commands that invoke the camera — like visual search or translation — will not save images or videos to your Gemini History. Industry observers note that warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear is available in three styles and a total of 14 variations. Alden, Reid, and Wren are inspired by the brand’s “most beloved silhouettes.” Pricing starts at $395 for optical and sun styles in Pine, Saddle, and Jet Black.

The Gentle Monster Intelligent Eyewear collection features six frames in bold colors like dark red, pink, gray, and yellow, with 16 total variations. They can be paired with tinted, clear, blue, or brown lenses, with prescription options available for most designs. Pricing starts at $449 and will be available in the US and South Korea.

Intelligent Eyewear can be used for contextual visual searches, asking Gemini about your day, and having it accomplish tasks.

Google Maps offers turn-by-turn directions, while there’s real-time Google Translate in over 70 languages.

Like on phones, Gemini Guided Vision “offers conversational audio descriptions to people with vision impairments.” This can be used to read fine print, identify color differences, find items, and explore unfamiliar places.

These glasses also serve as always-available headphones with support for YouTube Music, Spotify, Apple Music, and Audible. The Glasses companion app supports:.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Revision (Nov 16, 11:41 am ET): Microsoft has finally fixed the issues that took down most of its 365 services.
  • Update (Nov 13, 6:57 am ET): Microsoft claims recovery efforts are now in phases, with some affected infrastructure already back online and traffic slowly returning to normal.
  • Over a hundred thousand frustrated consumers were left with broken inboxes and unable to get work done as Microsoft Outlook went down on Thursday, November 12.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Revision (Nov 16, 11:41 am ET): Microsoft has finally fixed the issues that took down most of its 365 services.

Update (Nov 13, 6:57 am ET): Microsoft claims recovery efforts are now in phases, with some affected infrastructure already back online and traffic slowly returning to normal. Initially, the firm blamed high infrastructure loads across many regions, but the investigation eventually revealed a more specific problem with automated server health checks. The tech giant has revealed that automated server health checks misfired, kicking healthy infrastructure offline and triggering cascading connection failures across Exchange Online, Teams, and Copilot. There are automated health checks that can detect failing hardware and take it out of rotation before your inbox breaks. Instead, a particular server component that does those checks started failing its own tests. Multiple regions lost their healthy servers, and the rest of the infrastructure buckled under heavier-than-usual loads, preventing consumers around the world from loading their mailboxes or sending messages. Now, Microsoft’s recovery playbook relies on working around its referee. Engineers made a targeted change to work around the faulty health-check component on some servers to see if they would stay online, while rolling out safeguards to stop other machines from dropping out. Automated recovery systems have been activated to minimize the disruption, and teams are also working in parallel to rebuild the affected servers with previous configurations.

Over a hundred thousand frustrated consumers were left with broken inboxes and unable to get work done as Microsoft Outlook went down on Thursday, November 12.

Outlook users in the Americas began reporting they could not access their Exchange Online mailboxes, and the complaints were rolling in fast, with Downdetector reporting more than 125,000 complaints as of this writing.

According to recent reports, if you attempted to refresh your inbox only to be greeted by infinite loading screens, you were not the only one. Customers are reporting being completely locked out of their accounts across desktop apps, web browsers, and mobile clients. Microsoft’s official 365 Status account confirmed the hiccup on X, blaming Exchange Online, the cloud backbone that powers your Outlook email, calendar, and contacts.

We're investigating reports of people experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas. More details can be found in the Microsoft 365 admin center under EX1550543.November 12, 2026.

The company initially said the connection failures were limited to the Americas, but the company later confirmed that the connectivity bug could be hitting owners in just about any region.

The problem is due to the way Outlook clients authenticate and connect to Exchange Online mailboxes using different connection methods.

Microsoft engineers are currently scrambling to resolve problems on the server end and mitigate the impact, but the company has not yet provided a concrete timeline for a full fix.

Apps in Microsoft 365 that rely on the same service connectivity may also be slow or throw error codes until the dust settles, though Exchange Online takes the biggest hit. For now, the best course of action is to keep an eye on the official Microsoft 365 status feed, enjoy a rare, guilt-free excuse to ignore your boss’s emails, and wait for the servers to wake back up.

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1226 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While I acknowledge Meta’s role in bringing smart glasses to a mainstream audience, it has proven to be an irresponsible steward.
  • In a recent development, google’s second take on smart glasses is the exact opposite of what Meta has done.
  • Officially, Android XR glasses are known as Gentle Monster and Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While I acknowledge Meta’s role in bringing smart glasses to a mainstream audience, it has proven to be an irresponsible steward. Its “growth at all costs” mindset has actively poisoned people’s perception of the form factor. Under Meta’s watch, glasses have gained a creepy connotation before their utility has been fully realized.

In a recent development, google’s second take on smart glasses is the exact opposite of what Meta has done. Every single aspect has been considered, and the result is worthy of being most people’s introduction to the form factor.

Officially, Android XR glasses are known as Gentle Monster and Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear. The branding is a mouthful, and I’m not quite sure “Intelligent Eyewear” will take off. Something more colloquial, like “Google glasses” — glasses.google is the landing page — or “Samsung glasses,” will probably stick in the public consciousness.

That critique aside, the name reflects how Google wants Intelligent Eyewear to actually replace your existing glasses. Unlike the Ray-Ban trap that I frankly think Meta did not consider, Google’s offerings are not situational or activity-based devices like sunglasses. These are a “smart” upgrade to the assistive device some people have to wear.

As a wearable, smart glasses are a bit like smartwatches in that the platonic design is pretty well established and indistinguishable from traditional eyewear. Unlike watches, glasses are so visible on people’s faces that form overrides everything else.

In a recent development, fortunately, the Samsung hardware I wore for an hour last week looks and feels like glasses, almost unremarkably so. I’d venture to say that audio-only glasses without a display are a solved design challenge. Google emphasized that, at 41 grams, this is the lightest pair of smart glasses on the market, and it worked to make sure the weight is distributed evenly.

According to recent reports, the sides of the stems that face your head feature translucent plastic that lets you see the internal components. I liked that small design choice. You can control the glasses using voice commands, with Google debuting a fresh “Hey Gemini” hotword for the form factor. While “Hey Google” and “OK Google” remain available, the new one is meant to reflect how big a role Gemini plays on smart glasses.

Recent findings suggest that there is also a touchpad on the right stem that accepts taps and swipes, while a button up top lets you take pictures and record video. Another way you’ll be able to control the glasses is with your Pixel Watch and Galaxy Watch. You can play/pause audio and enable Gemini using double-pinch and wrist gestures. Notably, gesture support is also coming to the Fitbit Air next year.

According to recent reports, from its internal testing, Google tells me that which input method people use is pretty situational and ends up being natural. At the beginning of my demo, I favored the touchpad, but by the end, I was leaning toward voice commands.

Industry observers note that when you’re capturing media that gets saved, there will always be a white blinking indicator light. There’s also another light in your field of vision that’s analogous to the camera and microphone privacy indicators in the top-right corner of Android phones. When I first put on the glasses, that light was distracting, but I rapidly forgot about it by the end of my demo.

According to recent reports, talking to Intelligent Eyewear uses Gemini Live. Some prompts, like take a picture or play a song, are one-shot “chat” commands in phone parlance, but for the most part, you’re using Gemini’s back-and-forth conversation mode. Google heavily customized the Gemini Live model for glasses to reduce latency, shorten responses, and tightly integrate the camera.

Industry observers note that even compared to my last demo in May, the latency of voice commands has come a long way. That said, I need more time to see if it’s really fast enough to use as a primary interaction method for most commands.

It has been revealed that google built a number of privacy protections into Intelligent Eyewear that are clearly in response to the current perception of smart glasses. There are some interesting ideas here, starting with how Gemini queries that involve a picture (like a visual search) won’t be saved to your Gemini History, used for model training, or ad targeting. For example, if you ask Gemini to find out what kind of plant you’re looking at, that image won’t be accessible anywhere else.

Similarly, Google will blur all faces and filter out bystander voices before it gets uploaded to Gemini in the cloud. This on-device processing occurs on your phone.

Since that visual media isn’t being saved, the external indicator light won’t be active when you’re talking to Gemini. The LED is only on when photos or videos are being saved and can be reviewed later.

It has been revealed that that indicator light features anti-tamper detection that prevents recording. Algorithms detect whether the LED is covered by stickers or markers, with this process featuring hardware verification when the glasses are in their charging case.

Industry observers note that google’s “Glasses” companion app, with Samsung having a near-identical version for Galaxy phones, is pretty similar to the version for Pixel Watch. Unlike the bloated “Meta AI” app, it’s just for settings rather than the very definition of a growth hack with a full chatbot. The difference is staggering, and something Google deserves a bit of credit for in this age of throwing AI into every crevice of day-to-day smartphone usage.

Sources indicate that under the hood, the glasses are offloading a lot of processing to your phone. This includes HDR pipelines and video stabilization. The 12MP camera takes pictures in a 4:3 aspect ratio, while you can record up to 90 seconds of video. Images are transferred immediately to your phone over Wi-Fi, while videos wait until the glasses are charging to preserve battery life. I am so excited by point-of-view photography and the instantaneous capture the glasses offer, and early impressions of camera quality are positive.

Another thing I want to test is how Intelligent Eyewear fares as always-available headphones. There are two open-ear speakers and four microphones, and Google is clearly very proud of the noise-cancellation work in place.

As someone who has been waiting for smart glasses since 2012, I cannot overstate my annoyance at how Meta allowed smart glasses to gain a scummy undertone, if not overtone. It should have been more proactive to societal concerns. Meanwhile, Meta releasing glasses without a camera, thus removing the primary utility of real-world context, makes me deeply question its belief that this is the future.

Recent findings suggest that smart glasses that know what you’re interacting with in the world can be extremely useful. That always-available camera is a genuine physical advantage over smartphones. It unlocks new use cases and convenience that are just not possible with something that goes in your pocket.

Google took a long time to get back to glasses. From what I’ve used so far, the wait will be worth it. The hardware and designs are solid, while the software is chock-full of innovative, well-considered ideas.

#1320. Here’s how Google’s Android XR glasses are handling the camera & privacy

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (974 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5google ↗ Open Full Page

Here’s how Google’s Android XR glasses are handling the camera & privacy

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (974 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, google’s Intelligent Eyewear push with the first Android XR glasses from Warby Parker and Gentle Monster are forced into an unfortunate uphill battle.
  • In a recent development, to promptly summarize the problem at hand (and name names), Meta’s smart glasses developed a reputation of being abused by bad actors who would disable the visible privacy LED (which Meta only recently fixed) or use these glasses in tasteless ways.
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s a shame, because a camera in smart glasses serves such a functional role, both for the user in just capturing pictures and for the AI assistant built into the experience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, google’s Intelligent Eyewear push with the first Android XR glasses from Warby Parker and Gentle Monster are forced into an unfortunate uphill battle. The “perv glasses” stigma is very real because, frankly, early movers in this category didn’t respect privacy. Here’s how Android XR and Gemini are handling the camera and privacy on “Intelligent Eyewear,” and why I think Google has struck a near-perfect balance.

In a recent development, to promptly summarize the problem at hand (and name names), Meta’s smart glasses developed a reputation of being abused by bad actors who would disable the visible privacy LED (which Meta only recently fixed) or use these glasses in tasteless ways. Combine that with improper handling of recordings on Meta’s part and it’s a recipe for distrust and an earned social stigma. It’s not like Google is a simple bystander here, either. The original Google Glass project was met with the “Glasshole” stigma, and it’s something that Google has clearly learned a lot of lessons from.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a shame, because a camera in smart glasses serves such a functional role, both for the user in just capturing pictures and for the AI assistant built into the experience. I recently talked about how the camera was my favorite part of smart glasses in an glitch of our 9to5Google Weekender newsletter, but how it just feels a bit wrong now.

Anyway, with that context in mind, let’s look at how Google is handling this touchy subject.

It starts with the outward-facing light on every part of Android XR glasses, which works similarly to the privacy LED on Meta’s glasses. The key distinction here is this is a “recording light” on Android XR glasses. It turns on whenever the glasses are capturing content that can be viewed later in some form or fashion by the user. So if you’re taking a picture or recording a video, it lights up. If you’re just using Gemini for context, the light doesn’t activate. That’s because any camera captures being used for Gemini are deleted immediately after use. They won’t show up in your Gemini chat logs and that’s not a choice for the user – these images are purged immediately after they’ve been used so that you as the user nor Google can use them. That includes Google not using visuals from Gemini captures for AI training or advertising. Users also have control over what apps on Android XR glasses can use the camera.

Sources indicate that importantly, the light on each pair of Android XR glasses is also designed to avoid any tampering. Android XR glasses automatically perform a system check to ensure the light is working on a regular basis – you might catch the light blinking in white and blue while charging which is a part of the system check ensuring the hardware is fully functional. If the light is found not to be working, the camera is disabled.

One of the pieces of this package that really caught my attention is how Google is handling the privacy of those around you. When your Intelligent Eyewear glasses send a photo to Gemini, your phone automatically redacts faces from the image before it’s sent to Gemini. This happens locally on the phone, essentially as a part of the glasses app. Similarly, voice data sent to Gemini filters out other voices besides your own. The voice filtering bit is just one way in which Google is doing some impressive things with the microphones here, with another example being that the live translation feature works in a 60-degree “cone” in front of you, filtering out other voices in the space.

Continuing on with how the camera interacts with Gemini, Google explained in a conversation with 9to5Google that Gemini is tuned not to use the camera in cases where it’s not obvious that the user wants the camera to be active. An interaction such as “what painting is this” would very clearly imply that the user wants the glasses to view the scene in front of them and identify the art piece, where “how much money is on the table,” Google explained, would ask for a follow-up before using the camera seeing as it’s not obvious that the user expects the camera to be used in that sort of phrase.

Another way in which Android XR glasses will avoid the recording stigma is with their limits. Google is limiting Intelligent Eyewear video recording to 90-second sessions. While that does limit what the user can do, Google said that most recordings fell within that window anyway. Meta, by comparison, offers recordings up to 5 minutes.

Beyond just the glasses app and Gemini, Google indicates it is making other efforts across its ecosystem to protect against and deter misuse of the camera on Android XR glasses, including:.

Recent findings suggest that for the most part, Google’s efforts around privacy on Android XR glasses aren’t groundbreaking. This is how it should work. But seeing as the bar is exceptionally low thanks to a rough start from competitors, I found myself reassured and even a bit impressed by the messaging here – a clear explanation of the indicator light and the automatic on-device face redaction and deletion of Gemini imagery both go a long way.

Google’s sentiment around privacy on glasses is pretty nearly summed up by a sentence in its privacy post today: “…when technology can see the world around you, it has a responsibility to the people around you, too.”.

Sources indicate that google has slowly been integrating Gemini into pretty much every aspect of its apps and services. You can now find Gemini everywhere, from the best Android phones to Google services like Sheets, Gmail, and pretty much everything in between.

And with the company retiring Google Assistant last year, Google has been gradually switching everything over to Gemini. The launch of its first Android XR "Intelligent Eyewear" smart glasses yesterday is yet another example of that shift.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The latest Google Health app revision was supposed to bring a slew of performance improvements for some of the best fitness trackers, but instead, it unleashed a bug that's been plaguing Fitbit consumers for the past few days.

In a recent development, according to the slew of reports on Reddit, a number of basic health metrics have gone missing from the view in the mobile app on both Android and iOS, including overnight vitals such as resting heart rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature, and HRV. Google rolled out its 5.12 update last week, which appears to be the common link between user reports online.

Industry observers note that the bug isn't limited to just one device either — consumers on the newly introduced Fitbit Air and Fitbit Edge models, the Fitbit Charge 6, and Fitbit Sense 2 are all experiencing this absence. These vitals are tracked daily to establish patterns and highlight changes in your health, so if they miss a day or two, it could have a huge impact on your readings.

Sources indicate that but despite these health metrics vanishing from thin air, it doesn't necessarily mean that your device has stopped tracking your data altogether. In some user cases, the device has continued monitoring health patterns, but the app has just failed to display them.

Still, it's not ideal, and consumers have been quick to jump on Google's case — but the tech giant has issued some reassurance that it's looking into it.

Among the wave of reports on Reddit, one user went the extra mile and reached out to Google directly, sharing the email they received in response: 'it's a joke' they shared.

Other users turned to Google's support forum for answers, where one of Google's product experts remarked they had escalated the issue.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

However, the challenges in the app are persisting, and Google has yet to find a solution, leaving consumers to find their own workarounds for the time being.

One method you can try is simply logging out of the Google Health app and logging back in again. Some customers have found this helpful, but it hasn't been the golden ticket for others. In that case, try uninstalling the Google Health app altogether and redownloading it, which is a bit of a pain, but it's worth a shot.

We've reached out to Google for comment on the status of the issue.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's hard to believe that Spotify Wrapped is about to give us all a brutal reality check on how we soundtracked 2026.
  • If you thought it was too late to get in your final listening hours, fear not; Spotify hasn't stopped counting them yet.
  • The good news is that we still have between two and three weeks left before that day arrives, so if there was ever a good time to crack down on the final Wrapped preparations, it's now!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's hard to believe that Spotify Wrapped is about to give us all a brutal reality check on how we soundtracked 2026. Though the idea of it sends shivers through me, it's still one of the most anticipated and exciting events on the tech calendar.

If you thought it was too late to get in your final listening hours, fear not; Spotify hasn't stopped counting them yet. While we don't know when the exact cut-off is (Spotify's never disclosed it before, and the likelihood of it happening is slim), it's widely thought to be right up until the launch of Wrapped, which usually lands in late November or early December.

The good news is that we still have between two and three weeks left before that day arrives, so if there was ever a good time to crack down on the final Wrapped preparations, it's now!

For years, your Spotify Taste Profile has been sitting behind the algorithm, using your listening behaviors to determine which new music it recommends to you. While you can exclude individual songs and playlists from infiltrating your Taste Profile, that's pretty much it as far as controlling how Spotify understands you.

According to recent reports, thankfully, the platform brought Taste Profile to the forefront of the experience earlier this year, allowing you to see exactly how Spotify understands your listening habits and how it uses this to shape your recommendations, and to flag any mistakes it makes. Not only that, but you can also speak directly to it and actively shape what it feeds you.

In a recent development, using text prompts, you can ask your Taste Profile pretty much anything. If you want to explore a particular genre that's been on your list, you can prompt it to recommend more glam rock, experimental pop, or whatever you're feeling in the moment — and the same goes for artists.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

It has been revealed that if there's one thing that gets under my skin with music streaming apps is that, sometimes, you can run into artists you can't stand. No matter how much you try to ignore them, they're bound to crop up in your Discover Weekly or whenever you're listening to a Spotify-curated playlist — it's better to rid them completely, I say.

That's why I've gotten into the routine of blocking artists entirely from my feed. It's one of those features that, whenever I bring it up, others don't even know it exists. I'm here to tell you that it does, and it will change your life.

Recent findings suggest that all you need to do is head to an artist's page in the Spotify app, tap the three dots next to the 'Follow' button, and then select 'Don't play this artist'. Once that's enabled, their page will go gray, and their discography will disappear from playlists. Their music also won't show up in features like your Discover Weekly or Daylist, so your blocked artists won't get in the way of latest music discovery.

If you're on Spotify's Family strategy and your young kids can't keep out of your profile, then I feel for you. There's nothing worse than waiting all year for Wrapped to arrive only to find that your top songs and artists are from your kids' favorite TV reveals — the Family plan has individual profiles for a reason!

It's been difficult to avoid this in Wrapped's past, but rest assured Spotify has put its foot down on this infiltration this time around, and you can amend your settings to ensure this music stays far away from your Wrapped summary.

In your settings, you'll find a toggle that, when enabled, excludes all kids and family music that's played on your profile. Not only does this help with steering your Wrapped in a more accurate direction, but it also ensures that your kids' favorite music doesn't affect your recommendations, Discover Weekly, and Daily Mix — so it's not just a benefit for Wrapped.

Storage can be a constant problem if you're using a more budget-friendly or older device, but downloading the latest games doesn't mean you have to delete loads of pictures from your gallery or uninstall your favorite apps to create space.

That's because developer Level Infinite has just released a new version of PUBG Mobile designed specifically to be the lightest version of the popular battle royale game yet. The initial download of PUBG Mobile Flash takes up just 0.96GB, with multiple tools available to ensure subsequent content downloads are limited to the maps and modes you want to play – keeping as much free space on your phone as possible.

PUBG Mobile Flash also supports a wider range of devices than the base game, including those with just 2GB of RAM, and promises better graphics optimization for smoother frame rates.

The file size may be small, but Level Infinite makes it clear that this is still a fully fledged version of what it calls "one of the world’s most popular mobile games.".

It has been revealed that PUBG Mobile Flash players will be able to squad up with their friends on regular PUBG Mobile. There is also seamless account cross-progression, so you'll be able to pick up where you left off if you already play the regular version of the game.

“Expanding access to PUBG Mobile has always been an vital part of our long-term vision, and we’re continually looking for newly introduced ways to connect players around the world,” explained general manager and PUBG Mobile head Vincent Wang.

"With PUBG Mobile Flash, we’re taking another step towards that goal, making it easier for more players to enjoy the core PUBG Mobile experience, reconnect with friends, and remain part of our global community.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We're experiencing always-on tech fatigue, which is in part why wearables like smart rings and now screenless fitness and health trackers are becoming popular.
  • It has been revealed that they can capture all the same data as a smartwatch or traditional fitness tracker, but do so passively, in the background, so you can go about your day without distractions.
  • Android Central has tested many of the latest screenless fitness bands extensively, often sporting more than one at a time to compare and contrast them and the data they collect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We're experiencing always-on tech fatigue, which is in part why wearables like smart rings and now screenless fitness and health trackers are becoming popular.

It has been revealed that they can capture all the same data as a smartwatch or traditional fitness tracker, but do so passively, in the background, so you can go about your day without distractions. Screenless fitness trackers in particular are on the rise, graduating from a market once dominated only by Whoop to include huge brands like Google Fitbit and Garmin as well as smaller ones like Luna and Amazfit.

Android Central has tested many of the latest screenless fitness bands extensively, often sporting more than one at a time to compare and contrast them and the data they collect. At their core, they all do the same thing. But there are also notable differences in design, battery life, app experience, and subscription options (or membership requirements). You'll want to pick the right one to use alongside your Android device based on your needs, preferences, and budget.

The Google Fitbit Air is thin, comfortable, affordable, yet packs tons of power in a small band. Think Fitbit's history of accurate activity and sleep tracking combined with Google's knowledge in design, AI, and apps. With Google Health Premium, it's the best you can buy right now.

Recent findings suggest that the Garmin CIRQA is thicker and chunkier than others, but it's a solid choice if fitness is your main priority. That's thanks to accurate automatic tracking and a side button for rapidly triggering an activity, cute shareable post-workout cards, and decent battery life that keeps it going for more than a week per charge.

The Luna Band combines some of the best aspects of apps like Google Health Premium in a subscription-free, AI-driven experience. I loved the LifeOS system with the Luna Ring 2, and with the consistent app updates, it continues to improve, making this a promising option.

It has been revealed that you might need an executive-level salary to afford the Whoop MG's annual membership, but medical-grade ECG and blood pressure trends make it worthwhile for those with heart health concerns, especially. The app and system are among the most aggressive in terms of pushing you to get in shape, focus on your health, and slow the pace of aging. But for some, that's a good thing.

With features like live heart rate broadcasting to compatible devices like gym equipment and an optional arm sleeve, the Amazfit Helio Strap is meant for gym-goers and runners. It's a simple design with accurate data capture, and best of all, no subscription.

The Fitbit Air is one of the most accurate screenless fitness trackers, combining Fitbit's long history in the business with top-notch vitals and sleep tracking, along with Google's powerful processing and AI integration. While you can use the Fitbit Air with the free version of the app and get basic details, you will get a lot more out of it with a Google Health Premium subscription.

It has been revealed that AI Coach is one of the best I have used, answering questions about the data, like why you might not have slept well and what you can do to improve, what exercise would be good to work around a shoulder injury, and even logging specific dumbbell weights and reps to gather more details about a workout. I love how easy it is to log meals by either dictating what you just ate or snapping a photo. You'll see a detailed breakdown of calories consumed (versus burned), protein, fat, carbs, and more. It's a solid food diary if you want to use it for that, too.

It has been revealed that the companion app is easy to navigate with all the essentials at a glance, like heart rate, a detailed breakdown of sleep, blood oxygen, readiness score, and more. Most notably, the app guides you through how to tackle the day with commentary, analysis, motivation, suggestions, and advice. It really is like a virtual coach. A couple of massive omissions, our reviewer notes, are the lack of ECG and built-in GPS. But considering how affordable the band is, we can live with that.

Along with what's captured from the band, the more information you provide with food logging, details about workouts, injuries, moments of stress, and more, the more intelligent it becomes in putting this all together. It's one of the few wearables where I'd say the subscription is worth the money.

Given the affordable price of the band, use the three-month trial to get an idea of what Premium adds and decide from there. It's a no-brainer option to keep on top of fitness and vitals.

The Garmin CIRQA is thicker and wider than other bands, but it's still incredibly comfortable to wear. Most importantly, it tracks all the essentials for free. You can opt for the Garmin Connect+ subscription for add-ons like Garmin Coach, AI-powered insights, and nutrition tracking. But it's not robust enough to be worth it, and that's pretty much all that's behind a paywall.

Sources indicate that the band accurately tracks activity, vitals, and sleep; the data provided is typically in line with other wearables I rely on. What I love is that it's the only screenless band I have seen to date with a physical side button you can press to manually start and stop an activity. You can later clarify in the app what it was, like a cardio class or baseball game. But it does a pretty good job of automatically picking up activities with distinct movements, like walks, runs, boxing, and strength training. I love the ability to add a post-workout selfie to a cute card with workout stats you can share on social media or with friends.

If you're looking for a band mainly to track fitness, the Garmin CIRQA is a good option. You don't get all the bells and whistles that come with Google Health Premium and Fitbit Air. It's also a higher upfront cost for the band. But you can keep track of everything that matters, including a detailed diary of your workouts and stats.

One of the lesser-known brands in this space, Luna is best known for its smart rings. But the tech giant released its first screenless tracker at CES 2026 with the Luna Band, and it's a serious contender. It tracks all the same metrics as others and does so accurately, based on my month-plus of wearing it. This includes everything from activities to sleep, vitals like heart rate, HRV, stress, respiratory rate, and more.

Recent findings suggest that at the heart of the experience is the Life OS system, an AI-driven system that lets you ask questions, log things like stress and meals, get advice, dive deeper into data, and more. There's an "Ask Luna" hands-free voice option, though it's limited to iPhone support right now.

Seemingly inspired by Ultrahuman smart rings and the tech giant's PowerPlugs, the Luna app also includes downloadable micro apps you can add to customize the experience. These include, at the time of this writing, sleep alarm, cycle tracker, calorie tracker, and circadian rhythm. The app indicates that upcoming features are coming soon, like a Luna Age (cardio fitness score), supplement planner, and hydration analyzer.

The app has been updated and redesigned several times since I started wearing the band. So, if you are looking to get in with a brand that's experimenting and continuously developing, this is a good option. Most importantly, you can be confident that the data is accurate.

It has been revealed that around since 2015, Whoop isn't technically the originator of this category, but it has a similar reputation to Oura as the brand that put the category on the map. But before you get excited about a Whoop tracker, they're expensive with a capital "E." And the Whoop MG is the top-line model.

Recent findings suggest that it's a medical-grade tracker that, compared to its little sister, the Whoop 5.0, adds ECG and blood pressure insights. ECG is easy to measure any time by placing your thumb and index finger on the sensors on either side, and blood pressure requires an initial cuff measurement to then provide subsequent trend estimates.

The app is packed (and I really mean packed) with data that you might initially feel like you need a medical degree to interpret. Thankfully, however, it's thoughtfully laid out and explained to help you make sense of it all. It tracks all the expected metrics and has a Healthspan and Pace of Aging feature. After the 31-day logging period, it will report a Whoop Age that you can compare to your biological age and determine your pace of aging. It's a moving target, so if there's ever a stat that prompts you to work out, go for that walk, eat better, and head to bed early, it's that one.

In a recent development, if the Whoop MG is too rich for your blood and you are willing to forego ECG and blood pressure insights, consider the Whoop 5.0. Its membership options are slightly more affordable, but still more expensive than any other band over its lifetime.

According to recent reports, if you love the concept behind the WHOOP MG but find the pricing too rich for your blood, even for the WHOOP 5.0, the Hume Band 2.0 is worth considering. While I haven't yet tested this model (stay tuned!), it is widely praised for offering some of the same benefits as WHOOP bands, including a focus on longevity and helping you reduce the speed of aging.

According to recent reports, while you get the core tracking features for free, including sleep, recovery, strain, HRV, skin temperature, and of course activity tracking as well as blood pressure trends, there is a Hume Premium subscription tier that unlocks more. But it's much cheaper at $8.99 per month, which works out to be almost half the price of the cheapest WHOOP One blueprint.

The band and companion app capture useful data like metabolic capacity (similar to a readiness score), sleep apnea risk alerts, chronic illness detection (identifying early signs), and AI coaching with the subscription tier. You may have to take the data with a grain of salt. But the price of entry makes Hume Band 2.0 a good starting point if you're considering exploring the concept of a screenless tracker and value overall lifespan data more than daily metrics and workout stats.

According to recent reports, amazfit has a solid reputation in the smartwatch space, with many of its models ranking among the best affordable Android smartwatches. This reliability extends to the Amazfit Helio Strap, which is simple, affordable, and, based on customer feedback (we haven't reviewed this one yet), as reliable as its beloved smartwatches.

Sources indicate that one of the unique features is live heart rate broadcasting, which allows you to broadcast your heart rate to compatible devices, like a Garmin smartwatch, Apple Watch, or even gym equipment. The best part? There's no subscription required…for anything.

Industry observers note that there's a more premium option called the Amazfit Helio Strap Pro that boasts a dual-sensor system and is designed for hybrid athletes and HYROX training. But most people won't need that model. There are also useful accessories like an arm sleeve for wearing it around the bicep, something runners will appreciate so they can still wear a running watch on their wrist. This is a solid budget option for fitness enthusiasts who also want vital health tracking.

Choosing the right screenless fitness band comes down to two core things: recognizing your needs and budget.

It has been revealed that if you want something you only need to pay a single price for and that doesn't require recurring fees, choose one of those options. If you are serious about health, want guidance and granular data, and can afford it, you may find value in some subscription-based bands.

All these bands track both fitness and health, including vitals. But some focus more heavily on fitness, some on health, and some a mix of both. If you only want to monitor daily data, you can look for a simpler option. If you need guidance towards meeting goals, a more advanced one makes sense. For ECG readings, the Whoop MG is your only option in this category. If it's pricing doesn't meet your budget, however, you can consider a smartwatch with ECG instead.

Why you can trust Android Central Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

You'll be happy with any of these screenless fitness bands. For an AI-driven coaching experience, Fitbit Air can't be beat. But if you want to get something similar without a subscription, Luna Band is worth considering. If you exercise daily and want to track workouts as much as vitals, the Garmin CIRQA is a solid choice.

It has been revealed that the Whoop MG is a medical-grade device, ideal for serious athletes or someone who is especially concerned about heart health and/or blood pressure. But it comes in at executive-level pricing. It's worth noting that none of these trackers, even the Whoop MG, is a replacement for consultation from a medical professional, and they are not meant for diagnosis, only supplemental data.

According to recent reports, the best overall budget option is the Fitbit Air. It doesn't cost much upfront, and you can gauge how the subscription works through the three-month trial. Once the trial lapses, see the difference without it and decide from there if it's worth paying the nominal monthly fee. Even with Google Health Premium, the cost is one less takeout lunch a month when all is said and done. And even after a year, the overall cost is still less than the upfront cost of most of these other bands.

  • According to recent reports, “Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After this week’s Carbon availability, Google today unveiled Gemini 4 Hydrogen instead of keeping the “Flash” branding. This model is billed as bringing “cutting-edge intelligence to everyone.”.

Compared to Gemini 3.8 Flash (which debuted in September), Hydrogen is billed as a “major standalone upgrade” with “significant leaps in both speed and intelligence.” It offers native 1 million-token input and up to 1 million output tokens. Specifically:.

According to recent reports, “Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class.”.

In a recent development, in the Gemini app, Hydrogen is better at following and sticking to your tone, format, and rules, while offering clear tables and visual breakdowns. As such, “email drafts, study guides, rewrites, and documents come back ready to use on the first try.” Additionally, Hydrogen “more frequently calls the right tools (i.e., Connected Apps) and skills for the job.”.

In the model picker, 4 Hydrogen is billed as providing “Everyday help.”.

Free users in the Gemini app get access to Hydrogen via the “[Auto] model selection when it’s the appropriate model for the prompt.”.

Google states Hydrogen significantly upgrades Search (AI Mode) by better understanding your intent:.

…you can ask your question in your natural flow of thought — even if you have multiple parts to your query, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests — and Search will intelligently comprehend what you’re looking for.

Responses get more visual and will feature a wider range of relevant links. Hydrogen is the default model for AI Mode and is used for “your hardest questions” in AI Overviews.

This was a nice surprise when I opened the app an hour or two ago. It seems to be noticeably better, too.

In Google Antigravity, 4 Hydrogen has an “Extra” thinking tier alongside Low, Medium, and High. Then there’s Orchestrator: “Carbon that may offload routine steps to Hydrogen. Same Carbon-level quality, fewer tokens used.”.

To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity. Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session.

For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs.

For developers, Hydrogen costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.

‘It just looks like R2-D2’ — This new gaming phone offers flagship specs and PC game emulation at a killer price, but its design is something else

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (692 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidcentral

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Products aimed at hardcore gamers aren’t exactly known for subtlety.
  • Recent findings suggest that the upcoming Redmagic 12 Pro is no exception.
  • Sources indicate that although they do offer dynamic RGB lighting, all the marketing material reveals them lit up in bright blue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Products aimed at hardcore gamers aren’t exactly known for subtlety. Aggressive styling, bright RGB lighting, and bombastic colors are common whether you’re buying a gaming chair, a high-end controller, or even a dedicated gaming phone.

Recent findings suggest that the upcoming Redmagic 12 Pro is no exception. Its rectangular chassis is adorned with decorative elements and a smattering of colorful lights, designed to highlight its built-in liquid cooling. There’s a huge illuminated ring on the back panel, tracing the cooling loop that sits on top of the battery, along with a smaller rectangular shape and light bar next to the camera modules at the top, where the SoC is situated.

Sources indicate that although they do offer dynamic RGB lighting, all the marketing material reveals them lit up in bright blue. I’m sure it’s meant to make the phone look high-tech and futuristic, but honestly, it just looks like R2-D2 to me — especially that white model.

It’s a phone that makes a statement: “the person holding this is a gamer,” and while there’s definitely value in having a device that stands out from the crowd, I can already imagine the kind of looks that I would get pulling this massive, flashy bar out of my pocket on the subway.

It’s a shame, as the rest of the package looks like strong value given the $949 / £799 starting price.

Industry observers note that the phone is powered by the latest and greatest Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 and up to 16GB of RAM, the same configuration found in the considerably more expensive Motorola Signature 27 and other cutting-edge flagships. The liquid cooling system, which works in tandem with a powerful fan and vapor chamber, should facilitate more reliable and sustained performance than other similarly specced devices.

It’s a great combination given the gaming focus: early hands-on reviews already suggest that this is the fastest-performing Android phone at the moment, allowing for steady frame rates in extremely intensive games like Wuthering Waves at high graphics settings.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

You’ll be able to appreciate all of it on the 185Hz refresh rate screen that, while not the biggest or brightest out there (at 6.85 inches and 5,000 nits peak), should deliver butter-smooth motion in supported games.

This is also one of the few new phones to launch with an under-screen selfie camera, so you don't even need to worry about a camera cutout or punch hole blocking your view and getting in the way of the action.

You’re also getting some physical advantages that aren’t present on other phones, namely physical trigger buttons that can be mapped to in-game inputs, cutting down on the need for an external mobile gamepad.

It has been revealed that then there’s the PC game emulation. The Redmagic 12 Pro comes with built-in software designed for running PC games from your Steam library. Not game streaming — these titles are running directly on the hardware.

In a recent development, and no, the performance isn’t going to be perfect, and battery life will take a serious hit, but testers have already got titles like Red Dead Redemption 2 running relatively smoothly, which feels seriously cutting-edge and is not something that I ever thought I would see on mobile phone hardware. I just wish all of this goodness was packed in a less… attention-grabbing shell.

The Redmagic 12 Pro hits shelves on November 18, with early-bird discount vouchers and free gifts available for those who pre-order now.

Available now, Pebblebee’s latest Android Find Hub tracker color drop might also be the first real miss, with the festive theme falling short of what it’s supposed to look like.

Pebblebee has been dropping limited-time color variants of its Clip 5 tracker for Android Find Hub and Apple Find My all year, with the latest release this week including “Cranberry” and “Champagne.”.

It has been revealed that the fresh drop looks nice in marketing photos, but I will say, this is the first time I’ve felt the colors have missed the mark in person. “Cranberry” is a nice red color, but the bits of reflective sparkle shown in Pebblebee’s images don’t translate very well into real life. “Champagne” takes that a step further, with a very muted beige color that doesn’t have the shine seen in some of the listing photos.

They still look nice enough, just know you’re not getting the flashy, festive colors.

Industry observers note that the good news, though, is that you’re still getting the same core hardware. USB-C rechargeable battery, support for Android Find Hub and Apple Find My, 130dB siren, and more, all for the usual $34.99.

The previous “Hotline Pink” and “Techno Lime” are still available for a limited time, and Pebblebee’s website has a Black Friday sale live, offering 20-30% off when you buy multiple trackers and use the code “BFCM26” at checkout.
